original_quotes.quote: We formulate adaptive fast charging as a sequential decision-making problem in which a large language model (LLM) acts as the high-level policy of an intelligent battery-control agent in Fig 2 . The proposed method follows a two-stage supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization (SFT–GRPO) strategy. In the first stage, supervised fine-tuning teaches the LLM the structured battery-action protocol and initializes it with conservative expert charging behavior. In the second stage, GRPO improves the policy using one-step feedback from physics-based PyBaMM environments, thereby favoring actions that increase SOC rapidly while penalizing temperature, degradation, elapsed time, and safety-filter intervention. A deterministic safety layer remains outside the learned policy and constrains every action before it is applied to the battery model. This separation yields an agent that combines the contextual decision capability of an LLM with explicit physical feedback and non-learned operational safeguards.

B.1 Prompt review and a recorded proposal An independent reviewer checks candidate guidance against the cited episode summaries, reasoning, feedback, and images, including successful continuations that a new rule should preserve. The review examines whether the evidence supports the proposed failure mechanism, whether the trigger can be observed online, and whether the revision preserves task goals and the execution protocol. It uses historical interaction records without launching additional rollouts. Revisions that need further evidence return for refinement. The complete guidance bundle is automatically published after it passes review and replaces the corresponding prompt content in the next collection round. Recorded example: a keyboard-contact guidance proposal Existing guidance. Push in short segments, reassess displacement and rotation, and stop repeating a blocked approach. Interaction evidence. During table organization, the recorded review observes the fingertips crossing the keyboard border without visible keyboard displacement. Other inspected segments contain limited progress toward the required rotation. Proposed refinement. Separate missed edge engagement from contact that produces the wrong motion: adjust approach height in the former case and contact location in the latter, while preserving productive student pushes. Review outcome. The independent reviewer found that contact and height adjustments already occurred in the inspected execution, and requested stronger evidence connecting the difficulty to missing guidance. This candidate remained unpublished. The example shows how a broad operational instruction becomes a concrete, observation-conditioned proposal and how historical evidence determines whether that proposal enters the next guidance bundle.

original_quotes.quote: n indexed visual memory. The main VLM revisits object regions through inspect , using earlier observations to prepare a reflex or review its outcome. GUIDE.md records discovered mechanics, object roles, and strategies across episodes, while WORKING.md tracks current progress and observations that need further investigation. During interaction, the main VLM identifies operations that recur and benefit from a timely response, such as jumping over approaching cacti or steering toward a landing platform. It registers a reflex through set_reflex , supplying named reference crops 𝒞 ref \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{ref}} , search regions and cooldown settings ℛ kin \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{kin}} , and a Python guide function g guide g_{\mathrm{guide}} (Figure 3 a). The main VLM first inspects the relevant objects in a stored frame and then passes their exact frame references and bounding boxes to set_reflex . The detector consequently matches crops of the objects the main VLM has already observed and grounded. The guide function specifies when the recurring operation is useful and supplies a short instruction about how to respond. Crucially, g guide g_{\mathrm{guide}} cannot dispatch actions directly; it only decides whether to wake the reflex VLM and what instruction to pass. For a landing reflex in Doodle Jump , the instruction directs steering toward a solid green platform based on horizontal offset, condensing the main VLM’s learned strategy into guidance delivered when the event occurs.

3.5 Visual Feedback and Reflex Refinement For each reflex action, the harness retains the triggering observation and a Before/After visual record: a frame immediately before execution and an outcome frame captured after the input completes. These images are archived at native resolution alongside the selected action and its completion record. On its next turn, the main VLM receives a summary and can inspect both the scene that prompted the decision and the resulting change (Figure 3 d). The main VLM uses these observations to revise a reflex during ongoing interaction. After a late jump, it can increase the TTC threshold; after steering toward an unsuitable platform or firing on a distractor, it can replace a reference crop or revise the wording of g guide g_{\mathrm{guide}} . It records the lesson in GUIDE.md or WORKING.md and calls set_reflex to update the active registry. At episode boundaries, the engine saves the reflex library whenever the completed-episode score improves and provides restore_best to reload that checkpoint. Notes, visual history, and learned reflexes persist across episodes.

original_quotes.quote: C.2.2 Backend Integration We retain failure-driven SkillBank expansion and skill retrieval for SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . For ExpeL ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , we retain trajectory-based reflection, successful-experience retrieval, and insight-bank updates. The integrated interface names its operations Agree , Remove , Edit , and Add . For Shared Reflexion, we retain Reflexion’s failure-to-corrective-plan feedback mechanism ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) . The remaining changes are backend-specific. Our SkillRL integration excludes the supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning stages of the complete training pipeline. ExpeL’s experience gathering and insight extraction are interleaved with online task acquisition rather than executed as separate stages. Shared Reflexion extends task-local episodic memory to a cross-task retrievable memory. Consequently, the experiments evaluate SPG-Select with the skill-evolution mechanisms of SkillRL, ExpeL, and Shared Reflexion, rather than exact reproductions of their complete original pipelines.

Practice and evaluation. During practice, the task-selection policy selects a task and the agent makes one attempt using its current backend state. For each backend-benchmark comparison, every policy first receives the same N N warmup interactions. The backend state produced by this common warmup initializes the ensuing T T -round policy comparison. SPG-Select uses the observed outcome to compute the surrogate-progress feedback defined in Section 3 , namely the temporal difference between consecutive profile estimates. This feedback is computed from the outcome before the trajectory is used for the subsequent backend update. Actor-model parameters remain fixed, so adaptation takes place through accumulated skills, insights, or reflections. After practice, we freeze the resulting backend state and evaluate each held-out task with a single attempt. No updates or test-time reflection retries are performed during evaluation. This protocol measures the transfer of acquired knowledge to held-out tasks. Metrics. We report the terminal task success rate as a percentage of the evaluation pool. ALFWorld success is determined by the environment’s task-completion signal. WebShop success requires a terminal reward of 1.0 1.0 , and partial rewards do not count as successes. For WebShop, we also report Score, the mean terminal reward expressed as a percentage, which preserves partial credit. We additionally report ALFWorld results by task family to examine variation across task types. All reported gains are percentage-point differences computed from unrounded rates. Random seeds. The main results in Table 1 are reported as the mean and sample standard deviation across three random seeds. All other experimental figures and tables in the main text and appendix use a single fixed random seed shared across the compared methods. Skill-evolution backends. original_quotes.quote: Harness RSI. Following Meta-Harness ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , we optimize an executable harness H H around a fixed policy model M M . The harness determines the model’s context, tools, and execution flow. We write a setting as σ = ( M , 𝒳 ) \sigma=(M,\mathcal{X}) , with disjoint evolve and held-out evaluation sets 𝒳 evo \mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{evo}} and 𝒳 eval \mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{eval}} . The score J ⁡ ( H , M , 𝒳 ) J(H;M,\mathcal{X}) follows the benchmark’s aggregation rule (Appendix B ). Only evolve-set feedback is available for proposing edits, selecting candidates, updating SIM, or deciding when to stop. A run consists of N N rounds. At round t = 0 , … , N − 1 t=0,\ldots,N-1 , the evaluator executes H t H_{t} on 𝒳 evo \mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{evo}} and returns scores, traces, and errors as F t F_{t} . The proposer P P uses F t F_{t} and the run’s history 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} (earlier feedback and code diffs) to generate k k candidate harnesses 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} . The selector 𝒮 \mathcal{S} screens proposals before execution and chooses among the evaluated candidates, weighing performance, complexity, domain specificity, and regression risk: 𝒞 t \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{t} = P ⁡ ( H t , F t , 𝒟 t ) , \displaystyle=P(H_{t},F_{t},\mathcal{D}_{t}), (1) H t + 1 \displaystyle H_{t+1} = 𝒮 ⁡ ( H t , F t , 𝒞 t , F t 𝒞 ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{S}(H_{t},F_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t},F_{t}^{\mathcal{C}}), Here F t 𝒞 F_{t}^{\mathcal{C}} contains feedback from the candidates that passed screening and were executed. If no candidate is accepted, H t + 1 = H t H_{t+1}=H_{t} . The proposer and selector are LLM-based harness engineers; M M is the policy that executes the tasks.

3.2 Self-Improvement Memory SIM groups edits by the recurring harness problems they address. For a root-cause hypothesis c i c_{i} , such as premature completion, an entry is m i = ( c i , [ ( a i ​ j , o i ​ j , p i ​ j ) ] j ) , m_{i}=\big(c_{i},[(a_{ij},o_{ij},p_{ij})]_{j}\big), (2) where j j indexes attempts in order and ℳ t = { m i } \mathcal{M}_{t}=\{m_{i}\} is the current memory. Each attempt stores the modification and its rationale a i ​ j a_{ij} , predicted and observed task outcomes o i ​ j o_{ij} , and provenance p i ​ j p_{ij} (domain, benchmark, policy, and round). Predictions of which tasks an edit will fix are recorded before evaluation and checked afterward. At each round, the proposer receives the complete SIM in its system prompt, and the selector reads the same record when assessing candidates. Both read all entries without retrieval or truncation. The loop in Equation 1 becomes 𝒞 t \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{t} = P ⁡ ( H t , F t , 𝒟 t , ℳ t ) , \displaystyle=P(H_{t},F_{t},\mathcal{D}_{t};\mathcal{M}_{t}), (3) H t + 1 \displaystyle H_{t+1} = 𝒮 ⁡ ( H t , F t , 𝒞 t , F t 𝒞 , ℳ t ) . \displaystyle=\mathcal{S}(H_{t},F_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t},F_{t}^{\mathcal{C}};\mathcal{M}_{t}). Each proposal cites an existing root cause or names a new one. After selection, only the chosen candidate is recorded in e t e_{t} , including its measured outcomes even when the edit regresses or fails to fix a predicted task. The update ℳ t + 1 = U ⁡ ( ℳ t , e t ) \mathcal{M}_{t+1}=U(\mathcal{M}_{t},e_{t}) appends this record to the cited problem or creates a new entry, preserving earlier attempts. If no edit is accepted, e t = ∅ e_{t}=\emptyset and U ⁡ ( ℳ t , ∅ ) = ℳ t U(\mathcal{M}_{t},\emptyset)=\mathcal{M}_{t} . Entries with identical root-cause text are merged without dropping their histories. Appendix D.1 gives the entry-matching details.

Within our compute budget, independent RSI repetitions focus on coding; the other domains are evaluated with one run per condition. We study settings with compatible harness interfaces and keep the optimizer’s planning and search procedures fixed. Our comparisons evaluate SIM as a complete procedure, combining inherited memory with updates during target optimization.

original_quotes.quote: 3.1 Problem Setup and Overview As shown in Figure 2 , RoboCoEvo formulates the co-evolution of an agent and a policy as an iterative process. The base policy π 0 \pi_{0} is a robotic foundation model trained on reference demonstrations 𝒟 0 \mathcal{D}_{0} . In round i i , Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (Section 3.2 ) collects rollouts of the current policy π i \pi_{i} in a set of scenarios 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . An MLLM-based agent groups the recurring failures into failure modes (FMs) and writes or revises a detector d m d_{m} and a recovery program ρ m \rho_{m} for each FM. Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion (Section 3.3 ) then applies these programs to the detected failure states and to perturbed copies of them, which yields the corrective experience R i = f ⁡ ( π i , 𝒮 ) . R_{i}=f(\pi_{i},\mathcal{S}). The policy is then post-trained on 𝒟 0 \mathcal{D}_{0} and the corrective experience accumulated up to round i i to obtain π i + 1 \pi_{i+1} , whose rollouts are used in the next round. RoboCoEvo observes the scene primarily through a scene state s t = ( q t , { p t k } k ∈ 𝒪 , ℱ t , I t ) s_{t}=(q_{t},\{p^{k}_{t}\}_{k\in\mathcal{O}},\mathcal{F}_{t},I_{t}) , where I t I_{t} denotes the camera images. Here, q t q_{t} is the robot state, including the base pose and joint configuration, 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is the set of task-relevant objects, and p t k p^{k}_{t} is the pose of object k k . The symbolic state ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} is the set of facts that hold at step t t , such as open ⁡ ( k ) \mathrm{open}(k) , on ⁡ ( k , k ′ ) \mathrm{on}(k,k^{\prime}) , and held ⁡ ( k ) \mathrm{held}(k) . The agent derives and reconstructs these facts from the simulator state. Figure 2: The RoboCoEvo pipeline. Each round proceeds clockwise, starting with rollouts of the current policy π i \pi_{i} . Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (right): the agent identifies failure modes (FMs) from K K sampled failures and writes a detector d m d_{m} for each FM. The detectors localize failure states in all

Recovery program generation. For each FM, its detected preventive and corrective states are partitioned into development and held-out validation sets. The agent develops a shared failure recovery program ρ m \rho_{m} using simulator states restored from the development set. Following a code-as-policy approach, ρ m \rho_{m} is implemented as a finite-state machine over s t s_{t} that composes navigation and manipulation skills with planned motions ( Garrett et al., 2025 ; Sahoo et al., 2026 ) . Recovery success is defined as completion of the subtask at which the original execution failed. The program undergoes iterative refinement and is accepted only when its recovery success rate reaches at least 70 % 70\% on the held-out validation set. The recovery programs evolve alongside the policy. In each subsequent round, the agent develops new programs for newly identified FMs and refines existing programs for FMs that persist. These refinements aim to broaden the range of failure states that the programs can address, improve their recovery success rates, and more precisely target the weaknesses revealed by the current policy.

The accepted recovery program ρ m \rho_{m} is then executed from the detected failure states and from their perturbed copies without further agent intervention. Only successful recoveries are retained, and together they constitute the corrective experience R i R_{i} of round i i . Augmentation thus yields additional corrective experience from a limited number of observed failures, which reduces the number of rollouts required.

original_quotes.quote: We compare the stateless baseline with fourteen adaptation mechanisms, built from four ICL policies and two weight-update rules. ICL replays prior attempts as conversations, including environment observations and outcome feedback. Under a bounded token allowance, two retention policies determine how context is managed: FIFO evicts the oldest episodes to admit new ones, whereas Prefix stops admitting episodes after the first overflow. Two admission policies determine which attempts are eligible: All selects the highest-reward attempt from every round, even if it failed; Successful selects at most one successful attempt per task, from the first round that produces one.

GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) updates a persistent LoRA adapter ( Hu et al., 2022 ) from each round’s attempts: advantages are rewards relative to the round’s mean, and the loss is PPO’s clipped surrogate ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , without a KL penalty or standard-deviation normalization. SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026a ) trains a persistent LoRA adapter on the agent’s own attempts by minimizing the reverse KL divergence to a self-teacher’s next-token distributions, with no policy-gradient term. The self-teacher receives the agent’s original context augmented with a successful sibling attempt or, when none is available, the attempt’s feedback. Its weights start as the student’s and then track them as an exponential moving average. Each hybrid combines one ICL policy with one weight-update rule. Each round’s attempts feed both channels: the update trains the adapter on them, conditioned on the context they were generated with, and the ICL policy chooses which of them to keep in the context for later attempts. Appendix A gives the formal interfaces and losses.

Episodes contain actions, environment observations, and final outcome feedback, replayed oldest first between the system prompt and the current task. All admission selects the highest-reward attempt from each round, including failures. Successful admission selects at most one successful attempt per task, from the first round containing a success. It therefore changes both outcome filtering and the number of episodes a task may contribute. FIFO removes oldest whole episodes until the context fits; Prefix permanently stops admitting episodes at the first overflow. Neither uses summarization, retrieval, or an external judge. Reward ties, successful-attempt selection, and SDPO donor selection follow the trainer’s attempt order, which verl rearranges to balance sequence lengths.

original_quotes.quote: The procedure, S4, is pool-growing self-training ( Fig. 1 , detailed in Fig. 2 ). In each round the current champion proposes programs and predicts each four times; those it gets wrong at least once join a pool labelled by the interpreter, and a fresh adapter is trained from the base on the whole pool; each round adds twice as many programs as the last (300, 900 and 2100 in total). [RS25,RS26] The rounds share no parameters; the state that persists is the dataset.

S4 changed what S3’s records pointed at ( Section 4 ), and with it the schedule ( Fig. 2 ). Retraining from the base : generation g g ’s candidate is a fresh LoRA trained from the base on the union of every generation’s frontier, not a continuation of generation g − 1 g-1 ’s adapter; only the data of generation g g is new, proposed and predicted by generation g − 1 g-1 ’s champion. Frontier selection : a program enters when at least one of the champion’s 4 sampled predictions (temperature 1.0) is wrong, so the frontier also holds programs it usually gets right: one predicted right with probability 0.9 per sample enters with probability 0.34. [RS25,RS35] Schedule : 300, 600 and 1200 new programs per generation, two passes over the union, no separate replay, so the generations trained on 300, 900 and 2100 records for 75, 225 and 525 steps. [RS25,RS26] These changes were made together and no ablation separates them. Before any verdict, the examiner’s null replicate (base against base) found no discordant item, the base was served at the configuration under which it answers 12 exam items ( Appendix A ), and the examiner’s build was changed so that it identifies the declared base by the checkpoint’s content. With no default, the plain retry loop is the comparison. The coin runs only in simulated runs that carry a named simulator check; other synthetic runs never count, and simulated and real attempts are never mixed in one test. A pass on simulated evidence is a proposal: a person promotes the candidate, and the record says it was promoted on simulation evidence. A real robot never starts a task with an untested candidate. Demotion needs no test: a default whose real attempt ends in a protective stop or guard trip loses its place at once, and the default it replaced, recorded by the promotion, becomes the default again; with no predecessor the slot is empty and the retry loop runs. Forgetting and erasure. Three states per episode: full, compressed (only the fields consolidation and recall read) and abstracted (for an episode a decided procedure rests on: its deviations from the procedure’s sequence and a reference to it). Integrity is kept by a keyed hash, so deleting the key makes the evidence unverifiable. When an episode is erased, a candidate record is recomputed from the remaining ones; a decided record is corrected from the erased episode’s own outcome and dropped below the minimums, with an audit entry that names the record and the cause, never the person. Erasure always wins over retention.

The measurements are simulations; no real robot and no real users were involved. The memory rules were re-implemented in Python for the benchmarks and follow the specification, not the shipped code. The benchmarks of the tables below, the default-demotion replay and the router follow-ups were planned in writing before they ran, with hypotheses and pass criteria fixed in advance and not changed afterwards. Three measurements had no written plan: the capacity table through the production code, the width-and-shape runs and the vary measurement; numbers marked as found after a first look (the single large matrix on rewordings, the windows of the promotion test) are exploratory. Plans 2, 3 and 5 ran on the same kind of outcome table, and some of their hypotheses failed; the first table below is Plan 4.

(1) Over a finite candidate set this is equivalent to masking actions with G Σ = 0 G_{\Sigma}=0 before selection; in free-form action generation, a violating proposal is rejected at the execution interface and the trigger message is returned for replanning. Unlike gating in neural systems, the gate here is neither latent nor learned: its implementation and blocking semantics are fixed, and what evolves is the explicit specification Σ \Sigma . original_quotes.quote: Besides entries, the ledger keeps three kinds of records that are never retrieved: disputed values from less trusted sources, kept for audit; unconfirmed values, held until a trusted source states a value; and tombstones , which record that a slot was deleted but not its value.

Ledger deletion. For each affected slot, the ledger erases every entry, dispute and unconfirmed value recorded up to the request, past values included (I1). Each affected slot keeps a tombstone without its value. The extractor is never shown an erased stored record again; a value the user states after the request opens a new entry, while questions about earlier times still abstain.

Each store writes its full state, including tombstones and blocked ids, to one JSON file and can restore it; Ledger+Ep writes both stores to the same file. In our runs a snapshot is taken after every checkpoint; the file is not written atomically, and we did not test a crash during a write. All state is partitioned by user, and retrieval and deletion only touch the partition of the user id they are given (I7).

Each member s ∈ 𝒮 evo s\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{evo}} evolves during training through two complementary channels: its LoRA adapter ϕ s \phi_{s} is distilled from the investigator’s own calls, and its skill card, a short list of Report and Ignore rules appended to the role instruction q s q_{s} , is revised by a reflector model (Sec. 4.2 ). Visual artifacts are the cues that shift most rapidly as generators improve, and the calls issued by the investigator expose exactly the inputs, scopes, and difficulty levels on which the inspectors are consulted. The audio tools and the PaddleOCR detector remain fixed: their outputs are measurements, such as speaker attributes, transcripts, and text boxes, whose meaning should not drift while the investigator learns to interpret them, and the scarcity of labeled audio forgeries would make their adaptation unreliable. The investigator itself is optimized with reinforcement learning, so the system improves both in what it asks and in what it is told.

Skill-card evolution. Adapter updates change how an inspector perceives. Some failure modes, however, are better expressed as explicit reporting rules, for example that motion blur on fast-moving hands is not a structural defect, or that a soft object deforming under direct contact is not a physics violation. Alongside its adapter weights, each trainable inspector therefore carries a skill card [ 39 ] , a short list of Report and Ignore rules appended to its role instruction and seen by student and teacher. After each distillation round, a frozen reflector LLM reviews recent calls that the current inspector still judges wrongly, with their labels, and proposes rule edits. A candidate card replaces the current one only if it yields more correct verdicts on held-out recent calls without losing any correct verdict on either real or generated videos. This acceptance test makes card edits monotone on recent experience and prevents the reflector from trading false alarms for misses. Examples of evolved cards are given in Appendix D .

Synchronizing fast and slow updates. Training alternates rollout collection, investigator optimization, interaction selection, and periodic FSL refinement. Each batch is collected with the current main policy and a fixed inspector snapshot. After the investigator update, selected interactions enter role-specific queues. Every H H investigator steps, a synchronization barrier checks whether each queue contains enough examples to update its inspector. Eligible students are distilled, their skill cards are revised, and the new FSL snapshot is published before rollout collection resumes, while roles with insufficient examples retain their current parameters and keep their queues for the next barrier. This schedule lets the investigator learn between FSL updates while each refinement stage draws on accumulated interaction experience.

original_quotes.quote: Summary Models sometimes can tell that an eval is an alignment eval, not a capabilities eval (Needham & Edkins, 2025) . To figure out what features of an eval tell a model what kind of eval it’s in, we run investigator agents on a set of evals for both capabilities and alignment. We instruct these agents to explore the environment and probe what it’s evaluating. We find that investigator agents are increasingly able to tell capability and alignment evals apart, and that they do this by noticing that an environment “looks fake” and figuring out that a task is a “honeypot” designed to make an agent do something bad. Here, we’d make situations that mirrored the capability evals, RL environments, and deployment situations where we thought the model might try to escape the sandbox.
